slides.say: A B C D is a rectangle. E lies on A D, G lies on B C, and F lies on A B. A E is three times E D, and B G is three times G C. Triangles F E G and E G C are shaded. Which of the following additional data is sufficient to determine the total shaded area?
at: A B C D is a rectangle

slides.say: They ask which one piece of data, if they gave it to us, would be enough to calculate the shaded area. [short pause] We'll use the symmetry principle from the last lesson.

[short pause] First, the figure. A E is three times E D, so A D is cut into four equal parts, three and one. B C is cut the same way. So E and G are both three parts from the left side. That puts E exactly above G.

A D and B C are parallel, and A B is perpendicular to them. E G joins two points at the same distance from A B, so it's parallel to A B, and perpendicular to the bases. It cuts the rectangle into a left rectangle and a right rectangle. And F? Nobody told us where F is on A B. Remember that.
at: so it's parallel to A B

slides.say: Let's try choice number one, the area of E C D. They don't say how big it is, so let's call it s. It could be ten, or a hundred, any number.
E C is a diagonal of the right rectangle, so it cuts it into two equal halves. That means the shaded triangle E G C is also s, and the right rectangle is s plus s, two s.
at: the shaded triangle E G C
and the right rectangle is s plus s

slides.say: The left rectangle has the same height, and its base is three times longer, three to one. So it's three times as big, three times two s, which is six s.
at: The left rectangle has the same height

slides.say: And the shaded triangle F E G? Its base is E G, the whole side of the left rectangle, and its tip F is on the opposite side, A B. That's the symmetry principle again, so it's half of the left rectangle. Half of six s is three s.
at: And the shaded triangle F E G

slides.say: Together, the shaded area is s plus three s, four s. So if they give us the area of E C D, we can find the shaded area. In the exam, once we've understood this, we mark choice number one and move on.
at: the shaded area is s plus three s

slides.say: Some students see it even faster. The whole rectangle is six s plus two s, eight s. The shaded four s is half of it, and E C D is an eighth.
at: The whole rectangle is six s

slides.say: [pause] We're in a lesson, so let's see why the other choices fail. Choice number two, the area of A F E. Now s means a new area, the area of A F E. A F E is half of a small rectangle at the top, so that rectangle is two s.
at: Choice number two, the area of A F E
Now s means a new area
A F E is half of a small

slides.say: But how big is the rectangle under it? We can't know, because we don't know where F is.
at: how big is the rectangle under it
we don't know where F is

slides.say: Here are two allowed shapes. In both, A F and A E are the same, so A F E has the same area. But the second rectangle is taller, so its shaded area is bigger. So the area of A F E doesn't fix the shaded area. Choice number two is out.
at: But the second rectangle is taller

slides.say: Choice number three, the area of F B G, has exactly the same problem. We don't know where F is. It's out too.

And choice number four says none of the data is enough, but we already saw that the area of E C D is enough. So it's out, and choice number one is our answer. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: choice number one is our answer
